fixes.explanation: That's right, friend. The text says, "Now the leaders of the people settled in Jerusalem…" (Nehemiah 11:1). The rest of the people then cast lots to bring one out of ten to join them, while the other nine stayed in their own towns. I picture those leaders unpacking boxes in the holy city.

Good guess, since a city sounds like it needs guards. But the text never mentions royal guards moving in. It says the leaders of the people settled in Jerusalem (Nehemiah 11:1). The gatekeepers do show up later in the roll call, but they're a different group.

Tyre traders do show up later in Nehemiah (Nehemiah 13:16), but not in this passage. Here the text says "…the leaders of the people settled in Jerusalem…" (Nehemiah 11:1). These are Jerusalem's own folks moving in. No traders, no sales pitch, no "limited time offer."

Yes, friend. The text says the rest of the people "…cast lots to bring one out of ten to live in the holy city of Jerusalem…" (Nehemiah 11:1). Casting lots was a way of picking, kind of like drawing names. The other nine were to dwell in their own towns.

Right, friend. The text calls it "…the holy city of Jerusalem…" (Nehemiah 11:1). That's the name the writer gives the place these people are moving to. I'd say that's quite the address to write on a moving box.
Ancient is a fine word, but it's not the one the text uses here. It says "…the holy city of Jerusalem…" (Nehemiah 11:1). Holy is the name on this one.

That's right, friend. The text says, "And the people blessed all the men who volunteered to live in Jerusalem." (Nehemiah 11:2). These men volunteered, and the people blessed every one of them. I bet that felt like the cheer you'd get for saying "I'll bring the cookies."
